issues.passage: He agreed to spearhead the initiative only after every other department had finished its work.
issues.why: Valid natural use: someone can lead (spearhead) an initiative only after other departments finish preparatory work. Timing of start does not cancel the lead sense; a careful reader would accept the sentence.

fix.correctPassage: A small committee will spearhead fundraising for the new library wing.
wrongPassages: He agreed to spearhead the initiative by stepping aside so other departments could lead every decision.
Lobbyists worked to spearhead the reform bill by filing endless procedural delays.
Reviewers found the conclusion spearhead and unsupported by any of the data.

issues.passage: Officials rewrote the policy to elicit dissent before it could reach the press.
issues.why: "Elicit dissent" is correct usage (draw out a reaction). Odd political strategy does not make the verb wrong; a careful reader would accept the sentence as valid English.

fix.correctPassage: The interviewer's silence helped elicit a more candid answer from the witness.
wrongPassages: City council voted to elicit overnight parking near the transit station.
Officials moved to elicit the protesters from the hearing room before the vote.
Alumni were asked to elicit funds for the new scholarship endowment.
